lesson.child_mission: Materials are what objects are made from. Properties describe how materials behave (hard/soft, flexible/rigid, rough/smooth, transparent/opaque).
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same science idea to a new object or material, then compare two pieces of evidence for strength.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Compare a wooden block and a foam sponge: material names and two properties each.

FEEDBACK
Wood: hard/rigid (typical); foam: soft/flexible/squishy — accept accurate observed properties.

WATCH FOR
Naming the object (“cup”) instead of the material (“plastic”) skips the science focus.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Test ten classroom objects. Record object, material guess and three properties each. Sort into two property groups and name the sorting rule.

Write a short reflection naming one observation or step you corrected and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Materials are what objects are made from. Properties describe how materials behave (hard/soft, flexible/rigid, rough/smooth, transparent/opaque).
materials: Optional: safe everyday objects for observation
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.
lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Test ten classroom objects. Record object, material guess and three properties each. Sort into two property groups and name the sorting rule. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Original response on new material: Wood: hard/rigid (typical); foam: soft/flexible/squishy — accept accurate observed properties. Reasoning: I used material by attending to property and explain why it matters rather than copying the worked model.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: Naming the object (“cup”) instead of the material (“plastic”) skips the science focus. Correction: Wood: hard/rigid (typical); foam: soft/flexible/squishy — accept accurate observed properties. Why: the correction restores accurate use of material.

Parent: Likely misconception: Naming the object (“cup”) instead of the material (“plastic”) skips the science focus. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Investigate or describe a fresh example (not the worked objects) that uses material. Record evidence and explain how it supports your claim.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one science misconception about material, correct it with evidence, and say why the correction works.

Parent: Marking notes: Require a new example, named observations and a claim–evidence link. / Require misconception + corrected claim + evidence reason..

WORKED MODEL
A metal spoon is hard and rigid. A rubber band is flexible. Baking paper is flexible and can be opaque. Name the material and at least two properties.

teach_steps.explain:
Materials are what objects are made from. Properties describe how materials behave (hard/soft, flexible/rigid, rough/smooth, transparent/opaque).

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen or measured.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the observations, properties or test steps that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a result is uncertain, identify what would have to be observed or tested again. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
